title: Allocator invariant violation — kube-scheduler investigation (WIP)
content:
Summary:

This is a working investigation into an allocator invariant violation observed in kube-scheduler that correlated with large node resource oscillations across our GPU fleet. Symptoms manifested as repeated scheduling failures, bursty preemptions, and pods flapping between Pending -> Bound -> Failed with messages referencing resource accounting mismatch. Impact was intermittent but high-severity for customers on Dedicated pools; some inference workers reported CPU/oom throttling and request timeouts.

Why this doc exists: collect timeline, data, hypotheses, quick mitigations, and a recommended patch plan. Aim for a short-term mitigation we can apply to clusters and a longer-term fix to the allocator logic.

Impact snapshot:
- Window: 2024-11-06 02:10 - 2024-11-06 05:40 UTC (multiple smaller recurrences afterwards)
- Affected clusters: gpu-dedicated-prod-eu, gpu-dedicated-prod-us-west
- User-visible: 4 customer incidents (timeouts, job restarts), average tail latency increased 2.3x for short-running inference jobs during spikes
- Internal: SLO error budget consumed for two teams; autoscaler scaled up additional nodes which later drained and caused further instability

Detection and alerting:
- First alert: scheduler.bind_errors rate spike alert (threshold 10/min) fired at 02:12 UTC
- Supporting alerts: node.eviction_count, kubelet.eviction_threshold_fired, and prometheus rule scheduler_priority_failed_count increased
- On-call Slack: #eng-sre saw a flurry of messages linking to pods stuck in Pending with errors like "failed to admit pod: allocator invariant violated"

Initial timeline (high level):
- 02:10 - Node resource usage across a subset of GPU nodes begins oscillating: cpu usage jumping and reclaimable memory fluctuating.
- 02:12 - scheduler.bind_errors spike; new pods start Pending > Pending for minutes.
- 02:20 - Several nodes cross kubelet eviction soft thresholds; kubelet begins eviction scoring.
- 02:30 - Autoscaler reacts, launches extra nodes. Some nodes join with taints, others join late.
- 02:40 - Scheduler reports internal invariant violation in logs; a few preemption waves observed.
- 03:00 - Temporary mitigations: cordon noisy nodes, restart kube-scheduler on 2 control-plane replicas. Partial recovery but recurrence at 04:15 on other AZ.
- 05:40 - Second major recurrence; SRE focused mitigation executed (see mitigations).

Key logs and symptoms collected (representative excerpts):
- kube-scheduler log: "[error] allocator: invariant violation: nodeAllocatableTotal < sum(podRequests) after allocation for node/gpu-n1-usw-023"
- kubelet log on node gpu-n1-usw-023: "eviction manager: observed memory pressure: availableMemory < evictionThreshold, reclaimInProgress"
- pod event: "0/80 nodes are available: 5 node(s) had volume node affinity conflict, 12 Insufficient cpu, 63 Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu" (counts varied)

Hypotheses (ordered by plausibility):
1) Race between kubelet eviction and scheduler allocation accounting: kube-scheduler assumes nodeAllocatable values are stable for the duration of scheduling decisions. When kubelet aggressively evicts and updates Node.Status.capacity/allocatable concurrently, the scheduler's cached view becomes stale and the allocator ends up creating allocations that violate invariants (sum of podRequests > nodeAllocatable). This fits the logs and the timing with eviction spikes.
2) Node resource reporting jitter: autoscaler/OS-level drivers causing transient misreporting of GPU availability (nvidia driver restarts during node provisioning), leading to the scheduler seeing inflated GPU capacity, scheduling pods, then kubelet immediately reporting fewer GPUs.
3) A bug in the scheduler's scoring/allocate path for extended resources (nvidia.com/gpu) where preemption and resource release path doesn't correctly decrement internal accounting under preemption storms. Less likely based on code review but still possible.

Data supporting hypothesis #1:
- Correlation of kubelet eviction logs with allocator log timestamps down to seconds.
- When we cordoned nodes before kube-scheduler restarts, the best-effort recovery happened — suggests a state consistency issue rather than pure driver misreport.
- Metric snapshot: kube_scheduler_schedule_attempts{result="error"} spiked with matching kubelet_eviction_manager_events per node.

Investigations run (commands and outcomes):
- kubectl get nodes -o wide; looked for nodes with NotReady/OutOfDisk or unusual allocatable values. Found nodes with allocatable memory reported ~20% lower than usual during spike.
- kubectl describe pod <pending-pod> -> events show "allocator invariant violated" and also "node(s) had taints" in some cases.
- Pulled kube-scheduler logs from all masters; searched for "invariant violation" timestamps and compared to node kubelet logs. Matched evictions happening within 3–15s of error.
- Checked metrics: node_eviction_count and kube_scheduler_scheduling_attempts_by_result.

Quick mitigations applied (short-term, low-risk):
1) Cordon and drain the smallest set of nodes exhibiting persistent eviction to stop churn (applied to 3 nodes in eu cluster).
2) Raised soft eviction thresholds by +5% on the most noisy nodes as a temporary stopgap (kubelet config override via node config daemonset).
3) Restarted kube-scheduler on one control-plane replica to clear its in-memory caches (staggered restarts to avoid losing quorum).
4) Adjusted cluster-autoscaler warmup/scale-down delay to avoid simultaneous node joins/leaves for 20m.
Effect: partial reduction in event rate, but not eliminating recurrences.

Longer-term remediation ideas (investigation & dev):
A) Scheduler-side fixes:
- Make the allocator resilient to nodeAllocatable updates mid-decision: add re-check/compare and conservative backoff in allocate path (if nodeAllocatable decreased during decision, reject and reschedule).
- Improve metrics and counters: emit more detailed allocator accounting metrics (per-node attempted vs committed resources).
- Add an admission gating step: if node recently fired an eviction event (within X sec), treat node as temporarily ineligible.

B) Node/kubelet changes:
- Investigate why kubelet is evicting aggressively — tune eviction thresholds for GPU-heavy nodes and investigate swap/cgroups memory pressure patterns.
- Ensure GPU drivers are stable on node boot/provisioning; add driver readiness probe before marking nodes Ready.

C) Operational controls:
- Add a Prometheus rule to mark node as "unstable" when eviction_count > N in T window; used by scheduler/cluster-autoscaler decisions.
- Run a canary rollout for any kube-scheduler code change behind a feature flag.

Patch plan (immediate next steps):
- PR: add recheck of node allocatable at commit point in allocator (github PR link in linked artifacts). Requires unit tests and integration test that simulates concurrent node allocatable changes.
- Instrumentation: add kube_scheduler_allocator_attempts and allocator_rejections_due_to_allocatable_mismatch metrics.
- Testing: create synthetic test that simulates kubelet eviction event concurrently with schedule attempt; validate scheduler rejects allocation cleanly and retries.

Operational followups (owners + ETA):
- (Priya) Short-term kubelet soft eviction bump applied to noisy nodes — ETA 11/09 03:00 UTC — DONE (monitoring).
- (Ethan) Add alert rule for allocator invariant errors and kube-scheduler restart runbook — ETA 11/12 — IN PROGRESS.
- (Mei) File driver-stability checklist for GPU node provisioning and add readiness probe — ETA 11/20.
- (Eng-sre + Platform) Implement feature-flagged allocator recheck PR and run canary across one cluster — ETA target 12/01.

Runbook snippet (temporary):
- If allocator invariant error fires and customers report pod flapping:
  1) Identify nodes in last 15m with highest eviction_count: kubectl get nodes -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, evict: .status.conditions[]? | select(.type=="MemoryPressure") | .lastTransitionTime}' (quick heuristic)
  2) Cordon noisy nodes: kubectl cordon <node>
  3) If many control-plane logs show allocator invariant: restart kube-scheduler (staggered) on one replica at a time: systemctl restart kube-scheduler or kubectl rollout restart ds/kube-scheduler -n kube-system (depending on distro)
  4) If GPU driver flaps found, taint node and create ticket to replace node.

Open questions / unknowns to resolve:
- Why did some nodes report reduced allocatable memory before kubelet logged evictions? Is there a chain of events from driver crash -> cgroup reclaim to eviction? Need node-level trace artifacts.
- Is autoscaler contributing by adding nodes too quickly and causing scheduling races when new nodes join with partially available drivers?
- Could a scheduler config option (bindTimeout) be tuned to reduce commitments racing with node state changes?

Monitoring and validation plan post-fix:
- Add allocator-specific metrics and a Grafana dashboard to visualize attempted vs committed resources per node; alert on mismatch rate > 0.1% over 5m.
- Run a 48h soak on canary cluster with simulated eviction storms (using local chaos job) to validate allocator robustness.
- After patching, compare pre/post frequency of "invariant violation" logs and customer-visible errors.

Appendix: quick snippets captured during triage (sanitized):
- kube-scheduler excerpt: "I1106 02:40:12.489 allocator.go:421] attempted allocation: pod/my-app-abc for node/gpu-n1-usw-023 succeeded=false reason=allocatable-mismatch"
- kubelet excerpt: "I1106 02:40:10.312 eviction_manager.go:235 MemoryPressure: reclaimInProgress true, availableBytes=123456789"
- Prometheus query used: sum(rate(kube_scheduler_schedule_attempts[5m])) by (result) and increase(node_eviction_count[5m])

Notes to self: keep this doc as working scratchpad. Do not escalate remediation changes to platform without a small canary and test harness. Coordinate with Platform Eng before changing kubelet eviction defaults for Dedicated pools.

End of draft.
